description: Sorting algorithms decomposed. Comparison-based: merge, quick, heap, TimSort, introsort. Non-comparison: radix, counting, bucket. Each has its sweet spot. Quicksort's partition + random pivot. Mergesort's stable merge. TimSort's run detection. Introsort's hybrid strategy.

sub_mechanisms.name: comparison_count_lower_bound
sub_mechanisms.definition: Any comparison-based sort requires Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case. Proof via decision tree height.
sub_mechanisms.why: Information-theoretic: deciding which of n! permutations is correct requires log₂(n!) = Θ(n log n) bits of information. Comparisons give 1 bit each. No comparison sort can be asymptotically better.

sub_mechanisms.name: quicksort_partition
sub_mechanisms.definition: Choose pivot. Rearrange array so elements < pivot are left, > pivot are right. Pivot ends in its final position.
sub_mechanisms.why: The core operation of quicksort. After partition, recurse on left half + right half independently. Partition is O(n) in-place with two pointers walking toward each other.

sub_mechanisms.name: pivot_selection_strategy
sub_mechanisms.definition: First element (O(n²) on sorted input). Random (expected O(n log n)). Median-of-three (good in practice). Median-of-medians (O(n) worst case but high constant).
sub_mechanisms.why: Pivot choice determines partition balance. Bad choice = unbalanced partitions = O(n²). Random + median-of-three are the practical choices. Median-of-medians is theoretical (used in introsort as fallback).

sub_mechanisms.name: mergesort_merge
sub_mechanisms.definition: Merge two sorted arrays: two pointers, take smaller, advance. O(n) merge of two arrays totaling n.
sub_mechanisms.why: The merge is what makes mergesort work. Combined with divide-into-halves: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) → O(n log n). The merge requires auxiliary space O(n).

sub_mechanisms.name: mergesort_stable
sub_mechanisms.definition: Mergesort is stable: equal elements preserve original order. Achieved by taking from left array first on ties.
sub_mechanisms.why: Stability matters when sorting by multiple keys: stable sort by secondary then primary gives correct lexicographic. Mergesort is the canonical stable O(n log n) sort.

sub_mechanisms.name: timsort_run_detection
sub_mechanisms.definition: Scan input for sorted runs (ascending or descending). Reverse descending runs. Extend short runs with binary-insertion sort.
sub_mechanisms.why: Real-world data has natural sorted runs (mostly-sorted, partially-sorted). Exploiting them turns O(n log n) into O(n) on already-sorted input. Python + Java's default sort.

sub_mechanisms.name: timsort_merge_strategy
sub_mechanisms.definition: Use a stack of runs. Maintain invariants: run sizes form a Fibonacci-like sequence. Merge to restore invariant.
sub_mechanisms.why: Memory-efficient run management. Galloping mode accelerates merge when one run dominates. Complex but well-tuned for real-world data.

sub_mechanisms.name: introsort_depth_limit
sub_mechanisms.definition: Run quicksort. If recursion depth exceeds 2·log₂(n), switch to heapsort.
sub_mechanisms.why: Hybrid: quicksort's speed in common case + heapsort's worst-case guarantee. C++ std::sort. Depth limit detects pathological pivot choices (giving O(n²)) and bails out before degradation.

sub_mechanisms.name: introsort_insertion_threshold
sub_mechanisms.definition: Below ~16 elements, fall back to insertion sort.
sub_mechanisms.why: Insertion sort's low constant + cache-friendliness wins for small arrays. The threshold is empirically tuned per implementation. Hybrid approach exploits small-N regime.

sub_mechanisms.name: radix_sort_LSB
sub_mechanisms.definition: Sort by each digit, least significant first, using a stable sort per digit. For 32-bit integers, 4 passes of 8-bit counting sort.
sub_mechanisms.why: Linear time O(d·n) where d is digit count. Beats comparison sorts when keys are short. Used in some specialised contexts (high-throughput log processing, GPU sorting).

sub_mechanisms.name: counting_sort
sub_mechanisms.definition: Count occurrences of each value, then write them out in order. O(n + k) where k is value range.
sub_mechanisms.why: Linear when value range is small. Used as the per-digit sort in radix sort. Stable; in-place variants exist. Beats comparison sorts when k = O(n).

sub_mechanisms.name: in_place_vs_auxiliary
sub_mechanisms.definition: Quicksort + heapsort + insertion sort are in-place (O(log n) or O(1) auxiliary). Mergesort uses O(n) auxiliary. Trade-off.
sub_mechanisms.why: Memory-constrained environments (GPU shared memory, embedded systems) need in-place. Cache + bandwidth matter for big sorts. Some hybrid mergesorts use external memory (disk).

derivation_rules.name: comparison_sort_bounded_by_n_log_n
then: worst case is Ω(n log n)
derivation_rules.why: Decision tree must have n! leaves (one per output permutation). Height ≥ log₂(n!) = Θ(n log n). The bound is information-theoretic; no comparison sort can beat it asymptotically.

derivation_rules.name: random_pivot_makes_quicksort_expected_O_n_log_n
if: pivot is chosen uniformly at random
then: expected runtime is O(n log n)
derivation_rules.why: Expected partition balance is good. Even with bad luck on some recursions, the average behaves well. Standard analysis: expected comparisons ≤ 2n ln n. Eliminates adversarial worst-case.

derivation_rules.name: stable_sort_required_for_multi_key
if: sorting by multiple keys (primary then secondary)
derivation_rules.why: Unstable secondary sort scrambles the primary order. Multi-key sort = stable sort by least significant, then stable sort by next significant, etc. The 'stable' property is what makes multi-key composition work.

derivation_rules.name: radix_sort_linear_for_short_keys
if: keys have d digits where d is constant
derivation_rules.why: Each digit pass is O(n); d passes total. For 32-bit integers, d = 4 (8-bit digits). Linear time when keys are short enough that comparison-sort's Ω(n log n) is not asymptotically optimal.

derivation_rules.name: hybrid_sorts_win_via_small_input_specialisation
then: insertion sort beats divide-and-conquer sorts in practice
derivation_rules.why: Recursion overhead + cache eviction kill divide-and-conquer at small N. Insertion sort has minimal overhead + perfect cache behaviour. Introsort, TimSort, std::sort all use this specialisation.
